title: Heart chambers, valves and layers
blurb: Name the four chambers, four valves and the layers of the heart wall, and explain the "lub" and "dub".
question: Listening with a stethoscope, a student hears "lub-dub." Which valves closing make the "lub," and which chamber of the heart has the thickest muscular wall?

teach.body: The heart sits in the mediastinum, about the size of a fist, with its apex pointing down and to the left. Formally, it has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump blood out, with the interventricular septum dividing the ventricles. In plain English: the top rooms collect blood coming in, the bottom rooms push it out, and the right and left sides are two separate pumps working side by side.

teach.caption: Right side handles deoxygenated blood; left side handles oxygenated blood. The LV wall is the thickest.

teach.h: Why the left ventricle is thickest
teach.body: Wall thickness matches workload. The right ventricle only pushes blood next door to the lungs. The left ventricle must push blood through the entire body at much higher pressure, so its myocardium is the thickest of the four chambers. The atria, which only move blood a short way into the ventricles below, have the thinnest walls.

head: Layer
What it is
Note
teach.caption: The innermost layer, the endocardium, lines the chambers and covers the valves.
All four valves keep blood moving one way only.
Note the left ventricle's thick wall: it pumps to the whole body. Each AV valve sits between an atrium and the ventricle below it.
Left AV = Bicuspid; Right AV = Tricuspid. "Tri" comes before "bi" because blood visits the right side first.

teach.body: The AV valve cusps are tied to papillary muscles in the ventricle walls by cords called chordae tendineae. When the ventricles contract, these cords stop the cusps from everting (flipping back) into the atria. Heart sounds come from valves closing: S1, "lub," is the AV valves closing at the start of ventricular systole; S2, "dub," is the semilunar valves closing at the start of diastole.

Keisha, a nursing applicant, is handed a model heart and a stethoscope. She finds the thickest wall on the left ventricle and explains it pumps to the whole body. Listening to her lab partner, she hears "lub" as the tricuspid and mitral valves snap shut when the ventricles start to contract, then "dub" as the pulmonary and aortic valves close when the ventricles relax.

teach.text: Common swaps: the tricuspid is on the RIGHT and the mitral (bicuspid) is on the LEFT; the LEFT ventricle, not the right, has the thickest wall; and "lub" is the AV valves closing, not the semilunar valves.

items: Atria receive, ventricles pump; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.
Layers: pericardium, epicardium (visceral pericardium), myocardium (thickest), endocardium.
AV valves: tricuspid (right) and mitral or bicuspid (left), held by chordae tendineae.
Semilunar valves: pulmonary (RV to pulmonary trunk) and aortic (LV to aorta).
S1 "lub" = AV valves close; S2 "dub" = semilunar valves close.

summary: You can now place the four chambers, name the layers of the heart wall from outside in, and match each valve to its side and position. You can also explain the job of the chordae tendineae and which valve closures make the "lub" and "dub."

A.q: Which heart chamber has the thickest myocardium?
A.why: The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body at high pressure, so it has the thickest muscular wall.

whyNot.0: The right ventricle pumps only to the lungs at lower pressure, so its wall is thinner than the left's.
whyNot.1: The atria have thin walls; they only move blood into the ventricles below.
whyNot.2: The right atrium is a thin-walled receiving chamber.

A.q: The mitral valve lies between which two structures?
A.why: The mitral (bicuspid) valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and left ventricle.

whyNot.1: The valve between the right atrium and right ventricle is the tricuspid.
whyNot.2: The valve between the left ventricle and aorta is the aortic semilunar valve.
whyNot.3: The valve between the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk is the pulmonary semilunar valve.

A.q: Which layer of the heart wall is made of cardiac muscle and is the thickest?
A.why: The myocardium is the cardiac muscle layer, and it is the thickest layer of the heart wall.

whyNot.0: The endocardium is the thin inner lining of the chambers and valves.
whyNot.2: The epicardium (visceral pericardium) is the thin outer surface layer.
whyNot.3: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer sac around the heart, not muscle.

B.q: The first heart sound, S1 ("lub"), is produced by:
B.why: S1 is the tricuspid and mitral (AV) valves snapping shut as the ventricles begin to contract.

whyNot.0: Semilunar valves closing make S2, the "dub."
whyNot.1: Heart sounds come from valves closing, not opening.
whyNot.3: Atrial contraction does not make the "lub"; valve closure does.

B.q: What is the function of the chordae tendineae?
options: Stop AV valve cusps flipping into the atria
Carry electrical impulses to the ventricles
Anchor the semilunar valves to the aorta
Separate the left and right ventricles
B.why: Chordae tendineae tie the AV valve cusps to papillary muscles so the cusps do not evert into the atria when the ventricles contract.

whyNot.1: Impulses travel through the conduction system (bundle of His, Purkinje fibers), not the chordae.
whyNot.2: Chordae attach to the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral), not the semilunar valves.
whyNot.3: The interventricular septum separates the ventricles.

B.q: The epicardium is also known as the:
B.why: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium, lying directly on the heart surface.

whyNot.0: The parietal pericardium lines the inside of the pericardial sac, not the heart surface.
whyNot.1: The fibrous pericardium is the tough outermost sac.
whyNot.2: The endocardium is the innermost layer, lining the chambers.

C.q: Compared with the right ventricle, the left ventricle has a thicker wall because it:
options: Pumps blood to the lungs, which resist flow most
Pumps to the whole body at higher pressure
Receives blood from both venae cavae
Must hold blood while the atria contract
C.why: The left ventricle drives blood through the entire systemic circulation at higher pressure, so it needs the most muscle.

whyNot.0: Pumping to the lungs is the right ventricle's job, and it works at lower pressure.
whyNot.2: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium, not the left ventricle.
whyNot.3: Both ventricles fill while the atria contract; that does not explain the extra thickness.

C.q: As blood leaves the right ventricle, which valve does it pass through?
C.why: Blood leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary (semilunar) valve into the pulmonary trunk.

whyNot.0: The tricuspid valve is the ENTRY to the right ventricle, from the right atrium.
whyNot.1: The aortic valve is the exit from the LEFT ventricle.
whyNot.3: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle.

C.q: Which statement about the heart's valves is INCORRECT?
options: The aortic valve lies between the LA and LV
The tricuspid valve is an atrioventricular valve
The bicuspid valve is also called the mitral valve
Semilunar valves close to make the second sound
C.why: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle is the mitral (bicuspid). The aortic valve lies between the left ventricle and the aorta, so this statement is incorrect.

whyNot.1: This is correct: the tricuspid is the right AV valve.
whyNot.2: This is correct: bicuspid and mitral are two names for the left AV valve.
whyNot.3: This is correct: semilunar valve closure makes S2, "dub."

reteach.title: A two-story duplex
reteach.question: Imagine the heart as a duplex: two side-by-side homes, each with an upstairs and a downstairs. How do the rooms, doors and walls map onto the heart?

blocks.body: Each home has an upstairs room where visitors arrive (an atrium) and a downstairs room that sends them off (a ventricle). A one-way door connects upstairs to downstairs (an AV valve), and another one-way door leads outside (a semilunar valve). The right home sends visitors next door to the lungs; the left home sends them across the whole city, so its downstairs room needs the thickest, strongest walls.

blocks.text: Doors slamming make the sounds: inner doors (AV valves) slam first for "lub"; front doors (semilunar valves) slam second for "dub."

explain.body: The heart sits in the mediastinum, fist-sized, apex down and to the left. Atria receive blood, ventricles pump it out, and the interventricular septum separates the ventricles.

test.q: In the chest, the apex of the heart points:
test.why: The apex (the pointed tip formed by the ventricles) points down and to the left.

whyNot.0: The apex points downward; the broad base is the upper part.
whyNot.1: The heart tilts to the left, not the right.
whyNot.3: The apex points down and left, the opposite of up and right.

explain.body: From outside in: fibrous pericardium and parietal pericardium (the sac, with pericardial fluid), then the epicardium (visceral pericardium), the myocardium (cardiac muscle, thickest) and the endocardium (lines chambers and valves).

test.q: Which layer lines the inside of the heart chambers and covers the valves?
test.why: The endocardium is the smooth innermost layer lining the chambers and covering the valves.

whyNot.0: The myocardium is the middle muscle layer.
whyNot.1: The epicardium covers the OUTER surface of the heart.
whyNot.2: The parietal pericardium lines the pericardial sac, outside the heart wall.

explain.body: AV valves: tricuspid (right, RA to RV) and mitral or bicuspid (left, LA to LV). Semilunar valves: pulmonary (RV to pulmonary trunk) and aortic (LV to aorta).

test.q: Which pair are both semilunar valves?
test.why: The two semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves, at the exits of the ventricles.

whyNot.0: Tricuspid and mitral are both atrioventricular valves.
whyNot.2: The mitral is an AV valve; only the aortic in this pair is semilunar.
whyNot.3: The tricuspid is an AV valve; only the pulmonary in this pair is semilunar.

explain.body: Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles hold the AV cusps so they cannot evert. S1 "lub" = AV valves closing at the start of ventricular systole; S2 "dub" = semilunar valves closing at the start of diastole.

test.q: The second heart sound, S2 ("dub"), marks the start of:
test.why: S2 is the semilunar valves closing as the ventricles relax: the start of diastole.

whyNot.1: Ventricular systole begins with S1, when the AV valves close.
whyNot.2: Atrial contraction happens late in diastole and does not produce S2.
whyNot.3: AV valve closure produces S1, not S2.
